extracted.intended_audience: law scholars, employment-law practitioners, EEOC staff, and students studying Title VII and LGBT workplace protections
extracted.subtask_description: Legal-analysis of when employment actions qualify as discrimination "because of sex" under Title VII, the EEOC's interpretive role (including Macy v. Holder), and how those theories apply to transgender and sexual-orientation claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original Title VII protection (biological women)
rubrics_metrics.description: Early courts construed Title VII to protect biological women from employment discrimination on the basis of being women.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts initially read the statute conservatively—limiting protection to biological women—before expanding interpretations over time; examples include Bowe v. Colgate–Palmolive (sex-based seniority limits) and Gen. Electric Co. v. Gilbert (pregnancy benefits issue).

rubrics_metrics.name: Price Waterhouse sex stereotyping theory
rubrics_metrics.description: "Sex stereotyping": discriminating against an employee for transgressing gender norms (acting, dressing, or presenting in ways traditionally associated with the opposite sex) is discrimination "because of sex" under Title VII.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court in Price Waterhouse held that denial of partnership for exhibiting traits considered traditionally masculine constituted sex discrimination; courts look at whether an employer penalizes failure to conform to gender-based expectations or norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oncale principle — statutory prohibitions can extend beyond the principal evil
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory prohibitions often go beyond the principal evil Congress was concerned with and may cover reasonably comparable evils; courts may apply Title VII in contexts not foreseen by Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oncale v. Sundowner Offshore Services recognized that Congress's principal concerns do not limit the scope of statutory coverage; this supports judicial extension of Title VII protections beyond original congressional intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pregnancy Discrimination Act inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress amended Title VII in 1978 to state explicitly that the provision included discrimination on the basis of pregnancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This was the only meaningful congressional clarification of "because of sex" in Title VII amendments; it demonstrates that some substantive inclusions have been made by statute, while many other interpretive questions remained unresolved by Congress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual harassment / hostile work environment as sex discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: Sexual harassment that creates a hostile work environment is impermissible sex discrimination under Title VII even if it does not lead to economic injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meritor Sav. Bank v. Vinson recognized hostile-environment harassment as actionable sex discrimination; courts treat sexual harassment broadly as 'because of sex.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical judicial rejection of sexual-orientation as per se "because of sex"
rubrics_metrics.description: Many courts historically held that discrimination based on sexual orientation is not discrimination "because of sex" under Title VII.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases such as DeSantis v. Pacific Tel. & Tel. and Spearman v. Ford Motor Co. rejected attempts to bootstrap Title VII protection for homosexuals, reasoning that sexual-orientation discrimination affected males and females equally and therefore was not sex discrimination in the Hopkins sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial receptivity to transgender claims under sex-stereotyping
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have grown receptive to finding that discrimination against transgender people constitutes impermissible sex stereotyping under Title VII.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions such as Glenn v. Brumby, Schwenk v. Hartford, and Schroer v. Billington found that actions motivated by a failure to conform to gender expectations (e.g., firing someone for transitioning) are discrimination "because of sex."

rubrics_metrics.name: EEOC guidelines and judicial deference
rubrics_metrics.description: The EEOC issues guidelines interpreting Title VII; while such guidance lacks the force of binding statute, courts often afford it deference under doctrines like Chevron, Griggs, and Skidmore.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the EEOC is expressly delegated power to issue procedural rules (42 U.S.C. § 2000e-12(a)), courts have relied on EEOC guidelines for interpretation; the level of deference depends on the context (Chevron where agency has delegated rulemaking authority, Skidmore for informal guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: EEOC adjudicatory decisions and their precedential weight
rubrics_metrics.description: EEOC adjudicatory decisions vary in precedential effect: decisions of the full Commission are binding on federal-sector agencies and have precedential weight, whereas many Office of Federal Operations opinions are binding only on the parties and not binding on agencies generally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only the relatively small number (about thirty to fifty) of cases that reach the full Commission each year create binding precedent for federal agencies; OFO decisions can indicate "good practice" but lack the same force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Macy v. Holder holding: gender identity/transgender status is "because of sex"
rubrics_metrics.description: The full EEOC Commission held that "discrimination based on gender identity, change of sex, and/or transgender status" is discrimination "because of sex" under Title VII.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The EEOC in Macy employed two theories—traditional sex stereotyping and a new "per se because of sex" theory—to conclude that transgender individuals are protected under Title VII; Macy reversed prior EEOC positions that had excluded "transsexualism."

rubrics_metrics.name: "Per se because of sex" theory (as introduced in Macy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any employment decision that takes sex (gender) into account is per se sex discrimination under Title VII; employers may not take gender into account in hiring, firing, or other employment decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citing Hopkins language that "an employer may not take gender into account," the EEOC reasoned that if "gender's on the brain" or sex-linked evaluations play any part in decisionmaking, that constitutes disparate treatment "related to the sex of the victim"—thus making discrimination based on transgender status per se sex discrimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application/argument that Macy rationale extends to sexual orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Macy's sex-stereotyping and per se theories, the article argues that discrimination based on sexual orientation is also impermissible sex discrimination because sexual orientation necessarily involves consideration of the genders of the people involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author reasons that when an employer treats a person differently for being attracted to the same sex, the employer is necessarily taking the employee's gender into account (example: Pat attracted to Beth), so sexual-orientation discrimination will always involve gender-based decisionmaking and thus should be "per se because of sex" under Macy.
